voice: Direct, sober, historically grounded, and occasionally confrontational. Address the reader as someone who may be powerful, comfortable, or distracted, and who will die. Prefer honest questions and uncomfortable observations to encouragement. Never invent a quotation or attribute a saying without evidence.

entries.text: I came, I saw, I conquered.
entries.author: Julius Caesar
entries.work: reported by Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 37
entries.note: Reported as an inscription carried in Caesar's triumph; translation adapted.

entries.text: I found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble.
entries.author: Augustus

entries.text: Have I played my part well? Then applaud as I exit.
entries.author: Augustus
entries.note: Dying words as reported by Suetonius; translation adapted.

entries.text: What an artist the world is losing!
entries.author: Nero
entries.note: Dying words as reported by Suetonius; translation adapted.

entries.text: Woe is me, I think I am becoming a god.
entries.author: Vespasian
entries.note: Reported as Vespasian's dying remark; translation adapted.

entries.text: Let them hate me, so long as they fear me.
entries.author: Caligula
entries.note: Suetonius says Caligula often quoted this line, originally from the tragedian Accius.

entries.text: Julius Caesar was killed by senators who believed they were defending the Republic. The Republic did not return; within a generation, Augustus had made one-man rule permanent.
entries.source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 80-82; Plutarch, Life of Caesar 66; Appian, Civil Wars 2.117

entries.text: At the Lupercalia, Mark Antony offered Julius Caesar a diadem. Caesar refused it, perhaps because he did not want the crown, perhaps because he wanted the crowd to beg him to take it.
entries.source: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 61; Cicero, Philippics 2.84-87; Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 79

entries.text: The most famous line of Caesar's death, Et tu, Brute?, is Shakespeare's invention. Ancient sources report his last words differently, or not at all.
entries.source: Shakespeare, Julius Caesar 3.1; Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 82; Plutarch, Life of Caesar 66

entries.text: Marcus Aurelius, the philosopher-emperor, was succeeded by his son Commodus. The succession is often treated as a warning: wisdom does not automatically survive the person who practices it.
entries.source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 72; Historia Augusta, Life of Commodus

entries.text: For much of the second century, Rome was ruled by emperors who adopted capable successors rather than passing power to their sons. The system worked until Marcus Aurelius chose his son Commodus.
entries.source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 72.1; Edward Gibbon, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 4-5

entries.text: Diocletian divided the empire into four parts and then, unusually for an emperor, retired to grow cabbages. He watched the system he built collapse into civil war.
entries.source: Aurelius Victor, Liber de Caesaribus 39; Eutropius, Breviarium 9.26-28

entries.text: Hadrian addressed his departing soul as a little wandering, flattering guest, and asked where it would go now.
entries.author: Hadrian
entries.note: Paraphrase of Hadrian's dying poem; translation adapted.

entries.text: Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army and began a civil war. The river was small; the decision was not.
entries.source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 32; Plutarch, Life of Caesar 32

entries.text: They make a desert and call it peace.
entries.author: Tacitus
entries.note: Words Tacitus gives to the Caledonian leader Calgacus; translation adapted.

entries.text: The more corrupt the state, the more numerous its laws.
entries.author: Tacitus

entries.text: The people long eagerly for just two things: bread and circuses.
entries.author: Juvenal

entries.text: Who will guard the guards themselves?
entries.author: Juvenal

entries.text: Fortune favors the bold.
entries.author: Virgil

entries.text: Not to know what happened before you were born is to remain forever a child.
entries.author: Cicero

entries.text: Every empire believes its borders are natural until they move.
Power does not reveal character; it removes the reasons for hiding it.
The crowd that cheers your triumph today is rehearsing your funeral.
Ambition is a hunger that mistakes itself for purpose.
The more power people acquire, the less they can afford to be told the truth.
We build monuments to outlast us and then spend our lives maintaining them.
Every crown is a borrowed garment.
A person who cannot be alone with their thoughts will build an empire to avoid them.
What do you own that owns you?
If you would rule others, first learn how little you rule yourself.
You will not be remembered for what you intended.
The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
entries.author: Marcus Aurelius

entries.text: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
entries.author: Seneca

entries.text: It is not events that disturb people, it is their judgements concerning them.
entries.author: Epictetus

entries.text: First say to yourself what you would be, and then do what you have to do.
entries.author: Epictetus

entries.text: Epictetus taught that freedom is not the absence of constraint but the mastery of one's own will.
entries.author: Epictetus
entries.note: Paraphrase of Epictetus's account of freedom.

entries.text: The whole life of the philosopher is a preparation for death.
entries.author: Cicero

entries.text: No man ever steps in the same river twice.
entries.author: Heraclitus
entries.source: Heraclitus, as reported by Plato, Cratylus 402a, and Plutarch, On the E at Delphi 392b
entries.note: A later paraphrase of Heraclitus's river fragments, not a single verbatim quotation.

entries.text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
entries.author: Socrates, as reported by Plato
entries.note: Words Plato attributes to Socrates; translation adapted.

entries.text: All men by nature desire to know.
entries.author: Aristotle

entries.text: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit.
entries.author: Aristotle
entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics; wording popularized by Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926)
entries.note: A paraphrase, not a direct quotation. The familiar wording comes from Will Durant's summary.

entries.text: I am a man; I consider nothing human alien to me.
entries.author: Terence

entries.text: Man is a wolf to man.
entries.author: Plautus

entries.text: Philosophy is not a set of answers to admire. It is a practice of noticing what you would rather not see.
You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.
entries.author: Marcus Aurelius

entries.text: Think of yourself as dead. You have lived your life. Now take what is left and live it properly.
entries.author: Marcus Aurelius

entries.text: Soon you will have forgotten everything; soon everything will have forgotten you.
entries.author: Marcus Aurelius

entries.text: Marcus Aurelius noted that Alexander the Great and his mule driver died the same death.
entries.author: Marcus Aurelius
entries.note: Paraphrase of a passage comparing Alexander and his mule driver.

entries.text: Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow.
entries.author: Horace

entries.text: We are but dust and shadow.
entries.author: Horace

entries.text: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.
entries.author: Seneca

entries.text: While we are postponing, life speeds by.
entries.author: Seneca

entries.text: As is a tale, so is life: not how long it is, but how good it is, is what matters.
entries.author: Seneca

entries.text: The descent to the underworld is easy.
entries.author: Virgil
entries.note: Translation adapted. The line continues that the descent is easy; returning is the labor.

entries.text: Time is the devourer of all things.
entries.author: Ovid

entries.text: The phrase memento mori is not classical Roman. It becomes common in later Christian and medieval contexts, though the practice of reminding the powerful of death is ancient.
entries.source: Tertullian, Apologeticus 33.4; Mary Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)

entries.text: The story of a slave whispering memento mori into a triumphant general's ear is widely repeated, but the exact phrase is not attested in ancient sources. Tertullian describes a public slave riding in the chariot to remind the general that he was human.
entries.source: Tertullian, Apologeticus 33.4; Mary Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)

entries.text: You will be forgotten more thoroughly than you can imagine. The question is not whether this is sad, but what you will do before it happens.
If your achievements were erased from memory tomorrow, what would remain of you?
What are you protecting that will not survive you?
When you imagine your death, who is in the room, and what have you left unsaid?
The fear of death can prevent us from living; the awareness of death can teach us how.
The pursuit of permanence is one of the most temporary things about us.
You cannot conquer time by building something that lasts. You can only decide what deserves the time you have.
The dead do not envy the living. They simply stop.
The question is not whether you will die, but what you will have refused to face before then.
If a slave whispered remember you must die in your ear today, what would you change before evening?
The most dangerous lie is the one that flatters you.
Whose approval are you still waiting for, and will it matter?
The most useful thing you can know is the shape of your own ignorance.
Ask not what your legacy will say about you. Ask what you are willing to do when no one will remember.
The human capacity for self-deception is not a flaw at the edges of reason. It is one of the ways reason works.
Humility is not thinking less of yourself. It is seeing yourself at the correct scale.
You are not the center of the story you are telling.
Certainty is often a feeling, not a proof.
The need to be right is often stronger than the desire to understand.
You cannot learn from people you have already decided are beneath you.
You control less than you think, and you are responsible for more than you admit.
